A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniversalCEFR. Their main text, tables, figures, and appendices A–J support reliable comparison, including the complete prompt appendix. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual classification experiments, linguistic-feature correlations, and analyses by language, granularity, and text category.

after.justification: v2 retains the original classification experiments and reports revised aggregate correlations plus a new figure containing language-specific correlations.

M1.justification: The dataset-standardization procedure, 100-feature inventory, 23-feature subset, classifiers, fine-tuned models, and five prompting strategies remain unchanged. The complete prompt templates also match.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 26 source corpora, 13 languages, text granularities, learner/reference categories, and CEFR classification task. Welsh data and its collection procedure already appear in v1, including Appendix J.

E2.justification: v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 4 contain the same majority-class baseline, Random Forest and Logistic Regression configurations, ModernBERT, EuroBERT, XLM-R, Gemma 1, Gemma 3, and EuroLLM comparisons.

E3.justification: Dataset splits, the test-sampling cap, weighted F1 evaluation, three fine-tuning epochs, checkpoint selection, and Tables 17–18 settings are unchanged. The correlation procedures and thresholds presented prominently in v2 were already documented in v1 Appendix E.3.

E4.justification: The supporting evidence for which linguistic features track CEFR proficiency is substantially revised through extensive replacements, additions, and removals of correlations in Tables 20–21. Figure 2 adds a language-by-feature breakdown. The granularity, learner/reference, point-biserial, and language-specific analyses otherwise remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same random seed, correlation significance threshold, and mean/SD table structure. Changes to individual correlation means, SDs, and populated cells are result revisions; no new repeated-run, confidence-interval, or significance-testing practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 20–21 extensively revise numerical correlations: mean concreteness changes from 0.1429 to -0.4254, token count from -0.4254 to 0.5041, and past-tense ratio from 0.954 to 0.2782. Figure 2 adds language-specific coefficients. The matched classification-performance tables are unchanged.

T1.justification: No formal theory, theorem, proof, or derivation is added or removed. CEFR definitions and the existing correlation-analysis criteria are retained.

C1.justification: The principal dataset, standardization, and empirical contribution claims remain unchanged. The conclusion adds a modest scope qualification, restricting its final claim about mitigating the linguistic Matthew effect to language-proficiency assessment research.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly qualifies the pooled evaluation across text formats and categories and calls for dedicated category-specific modeling. It adds a compute-budget explanation for model selection and more concrete recommendations for expanding scarce data and improving features for morphologically rich languages.

D1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the stated dataset status from availability after review to current availability and replaces the generic Hugging Face library link with the UniversalCEFR dataset-collection link. Table 21 also adds TSEval to the verb–noun-ratio resource attribution; experimental settings remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Paquot et al. (2024) and discusses CLARIN's LC-meta schema in the background on data standardization. The remaining literature coverage and research positioning are largely retained.

P1.justification: Linguistic Feature Analysis becomes standalone Section 4 with two subsections, reusing material retained in Appendix E.3. v2 also copyedits prose, revises limitations, and renumbers subsequent sections without broadly restructuring the paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds the correlation heatmap in Figure 2, relocates v1 Appendix Table 6 to main-text Table 3, and introduces category shading in Table 20. Other changes chiefly concern table ordering, numbering, and page flow; the prompt layouts remain essentially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves internal consistency: revised Table 20 reports negative concreteness and imageability correlations, matching the interpretation that v1's positive means contradicted. The new heatmap, clearer limitations of pooled evaluation, and improved access information strengthen interpretability and usability. These gains concern supporting analysis and reporting; the central resource and benchmark evidence remain unchanged.
